paragraphs.text: This cake holds leaf from Yiwu, in Yunnan, taken through the [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) process and pressed once its fermentation was done. Ripe pu’er was devised to give, in weeks, what Hong Kong and Guangdong drinkers had known from raw pu’er kept for years, so a ripe cake is ready to drink soon after it is made rather than after a long wait.

The fermentation is [wet piling](shou:wet-piling): sun-dried leaf is wetted and heaped so heat, moisture and microbes can work on it. The microbes make the heat themselves, so the pile is covered to hold it in, then turned about once a week to spread it and let air in. It is kept below about 65°C, because hotter than that the leaf begins to char, and after one to two months the leaf is dried.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
